To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of wearable sensors to monitor Parkinson's disease symptoms can be simplified without sacrificing accuracy.

1) the gyroscope signal is more informative than the accelerometer for bradykinesic movement classification, 2) the sampling frequency of the accelerometer and gyroscope signals can be decreased to 62. 5 Hz and 31. 25 Hz, respectively, while maintaining the classification performance, 3) the classification performance of the accelerometer and gyroscopic features can be maintained even when the feature set is substantially reduced, and 4) the performance of the flexible sensor is similar to

the use of a flexible sensor with tri axial accelerometer and gyroscopic sensors and sampling at 31.25 Hz is optimal for the detection of tremor and that a smart watch with a tri axial accelerometer sensor and sampling at 125 Hz is optimal for detecting bradykinesi.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of wearable sensors to monitor the progression of PD and to identify individuals at risk of developing PD.
the role of data resolution in the accurate detection and monitoring of PD symptoms.
understanding the relationship between data resolution and accuracy when using body worn sensor data to classify Parkinson's disease symptoms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the data measurement characteristics of the wearable sensor used to monitor Parkinson's disease symptoms are not as important as the type and amount of features used to classify these symptoms.
this study demonstrates that wearable sensor data can be simplified to reduce computational burden, while maintaining performance for the detection of tremor and Bradykinesia in PD.
the role of data measurement characteristics (sampling rate and features) on the accurate detection of PD symptoms using wearable sensors is dependent on symptom type and sensor type.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found that using a smartwatch to detect PD motor symptoms is as accurate as using an advanced wearable sensor.
we can detect PD symptoms with a smartwatch, and that we can do this with a much smaller set of features than previously used, and at a much lower sampling rate.
the more data that is collected, the more features that are extracted from the data, the better the performance of the machine learning model.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to simplify the measurement characteristics from body-worn sensors while maintaining performance for PD symptom detection.
it is possible to reduce the amount of data collected by wearable sensor systems without compromising performance.
the accuracy of symptom detection models can be maintained by reducing the sampling rate of the data and the complexity of the features.
